questions.stem: In an N-type semiconductor, what are the majority charge carriers and which category of impurity element provides them?

options.option_text: Holes, provided by trivalent impurities such as boron or aluminium
Free electrons, provided by pentavalent impurities such as phosphorus
Electron-hole pairs, generated by thermal energy within the crystal lattice
Positive ions, formed when donor atoms permanently lose electrons to the lattice

questions.explanation: B is correct. Pentavalent dopants (5 valence electrons) such as phosphorus, arsenic, or antimony form four covalent bonds with neighbouring silicon atoms and donate their fifth electron as a free carrier. These donated free electrons become the majority carriers in N-type material. Option A describes P-type semiconductors where trivalent dopants create electron vacancies (holes). Option D is wrong because the donor ions are fixed in the lattice after donating their electron — they are immobile and do not carry current.

questions.stem: A Zener diode is specifically designed to operate in which region of its I-V characteristic, and for what primary circuit application?

options.option_text: Forward bias region, to emit light proportional to the forward current flowing
Reverse breakdown region, to maintain a constant reference voltage output
Forward bias region, to rectify alternating current into pulsating direct current
Reverse bias region, to amplify weak electrical signals with high voltage gain

questions.explanation: B is correct. A Zener diode is heavily doped so that reverse breakdown occurs at a precise, well-defined voltage (Zener voltage). Once in breakdown, the voltage across it remains nearly constant despite varying current — making it the standard circuit element for voltage regulation and reference. Option A describes an LED (forward bias + photon emission). Option C describes a rectifier diode used in power supplies. Option D is wrong — a reverse-biased diode in the pre-breakdown region carries only negligible leakage current and cannot amplify.

questions.stem: The depletion region at a P-N junction is called 'depleted' because it is depleted of which of the following?

options.option_text: Fixed donor and acceptor ions that have migrated toward the junction boundary
Mobile charge carriers — free electrons and holes — that recombined across it
Covalent bonds that break under the influence of the built-in electric field
Valence electrons released from broken covalent bonds by thermal excitation alone

questions.explanation: B is correct. When the P and N regions are brought together, holes from the P-side diffuse into the N-side and electrons from the N-side diffuse into the P-side; they recombine and annihilate each other near the junction. The resulting zone is depleted of mobile carriers (free electrons and holes), leaving behind only fixed space charges. Option A is wrong because the fixed ions do NOT migrate — they remain in place and are exactly what creates the built-in electric field. Option C is wrong — covalent bonds are not broken by the built-in field at equilibrium; bond breaking is a thermal/optical process.

questions.stem: Modern electronics overwhelmingly uses silicon rather than germanium as the base semiconductor material. The PRIMARY reason is that silicon:

options.option_text: Has a wider bandgap (1.1 eV) than germanium, ensuring greater thermal stability
Conducts electricity more efficiently than germanium at standard room temperature
Has higher electron mobility than germanium across all temperature ranges
Requires lower forward threshold voltage, reducing power losses in circuits

questions.explanation: A is correct. Silicon's bandgap of 1.1 eV versus germanium's 0.67 eV means far fewer thermally generated carriers at elevated temperatures, allowing silicon devices to operate reliably up to ~150 °C compared to ~75 °C for germanium. Option B is wrong — germanium is actually a somewhat better conductor at room temperature precisely because its narrower bandgap creates more intrinsic carriers. Option C is wrong — germanium has higher electron mobility (~3900 cm²/V·s vs ~1500 for silicon). Option D is wrong — silicon requires a ~0.7 V forward drop, while germanium only needs ~0.3 V, so it is germanium that has the lower threshold.

questions.stem: In a common-emitter (CE) BJT amplifier, what is the phase relationship between the input signal at the base and the voltage output taken at the collector?

options.option_text: In phase (0°), which is why CE configuration is used in unity-gain buffer stages
180° out of phase (inverted), making CE the standard choice for voltage amplification
90° out of phase, because the transistor acts as a reactive component at signal frequencies
In phase (0°), due to positive feedback established within the emitter-base loop

questions.explanation: B is correct. In CE configuration, when input voltage at the base rises (positive half-cycle), base current and therefore collector current increase. The larger collector current causes a greater voltage drop across the collector resistor, so the collector voltage falls — producing an inverted (180° phase-shifted) output. This inversion is the hallmark of CE amplifiers, which also give high voltage and power gain. Option A is wrong — unity voltage gain (≈1) with no phase inversion is the signature of the common-collector (emitter-follower) configuration. Option C is wrong — 90° phase shift is characteristic of reactive (capacitive/inductive) circuits, not BJT amplifiers at mid-band.

questions.stem: A silicon BJT has a DC current transfer ratio α (alpha) of 0.98 in common-base configuration. What is its approximate current gain β (beta) in common-emitter configuration?

options.option_text: β ≈ 49, calculated from the relation β = α ÷ (1 − α) = 0.98 ÷ 0.02
β ≈ 0.98, because alpha and beta are equivalent parameters in different configurations
β ≈ 196, since beta equals four times the value of alpha for silicon transistors
β ≈ 1.02, obtained by taking the reciprocal of α, since beta is defined as 1 ÷ α

questions.explanation: A is correct. The exact relation between common-base gain α and common-emitter gain β is: β = α/(1−α). Substituting: β = 0.98/(1−0.98) = 0.98/0.02 = 49. This result is consistent with the physical fact that α < 1 always, while β is typically 20–500 for silicon transistors. Option B confuses α and β — they are numerically very different; α is the fraction of emitter current reaching the collector (always < 1), while β is the ratio of collector to base current (much > 1). Option C (β ≈ 196) would arise from the incorrect formula β = 4α. Option D (β ≈ 1.02) comes from mistakenly computing 1/α = 1/0.98 ≈ 1.02, which gives γ (emitter injection efficiency), not β.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes how avalanche breakdown differs from Zener breakdown in a reverse-biased P-N diode?

options.option_text: Avalanche uses impact ionisation at voltages above ~6 V and has a positive temperature coefficient
Zener breakdown occurs at higher voltages than avalanche due to needing a stronger electric field
Avalanche uses quantum tunnelling at low voltages in heavily doped, thin-junction diodes
Zener breakdown is irreversible and permanently damages the diode, unlike avalanche

questions.explanation: A is correct. In avalanche breakdown (typically >6 V), thermally generated carriers are accelerated by the strong reverse field, gain enough kinetic energy to collide with and ionise lattice atoms, releasing more carriers — a multiplicative avalanche. Higher temperature gives carriers more kinetic energy from phonon collisions, so the breakdown voltage rises with temperature (positive temperature coefficient). Zener breakdown (<4–6 V) relies on quantum-mechanical tunnelling of valence electrons directly across the thin depletion region of a heavily doped junction; its breakdown voltage falls slightly with rising temperature (negative coefficient). Option B is wrong — it reverses the voltage ranges; Zener occurs at lower voltages, avalanche at higher. Option C is wrong — quantum tunnelling is the Zener mechanism, not the avalanche mechanism. Option D is wrong — both mechanisms are reversible provided the power dissipation is limited; Zener diodes are routinely operated in breakdown without damage.

questions.stem: Germanium dominated early transistor technology, but silicon eventually replaced it as the preferred semiconductor for most electronic devices. Which property of silicon PRIMARILY explains this transition?

options.option_text: Silicon's band gap of 1.1 eV vs germanium's 0.67 eV ensures better thermal stability
Silicon has higher electron mobility than germanium, enabling faster device switching
Silicon is far more abundant in Earth's crust than germanium, reducing material costs
Germanium requires higher forward bias voltage than silicon for standard operation

questions.explanation: A is correct. Silicon's wider band gap (1.1 eV vs Ge's 0.67 eV) means far fewer thermally generated electron-hole pairs at room temperature, drastically reducing leakage current. Silicon devices reliably operate up to ~150°C vs ~75°C for germanium. Option B is the most tempting distractor but is factually reversed — germanium actually has HIGHER electron mobility (~3900 cm²/Vs) than silicon (~1400 cm²/Vs). Option C (abundance/cost) is true but is a secondary economic reason, not the primary electronic one. Option D is backwards: germanium's forward bias threshold (~0.3 V) is actually lower than silicon's (~0.7 V).

questions.stem: In a full-wave bridge rectifier circuit used to convert AC to DC, how many diodes are required, and what advantage does it hold over a half-wave rectifier?

options.option_text: Two diodes; produces output in both AC half-cycles unlike the half-wave design
Four diodes; delivers smoother DC with a lower ripple factor than half-wave type
Six diodes; enables three-phase rectification suitable for industrial power supply
Four diodes; requires a center-tapped transformer, unlike the half-wave rectifier

questions.explanation: B is correct. A bridge rectifier uses 4 diodes arranged so that during both half-cycles of AC input, a different pair conducts, utilizing the full wave. Its ripple factor is ~0.48 compared to ~1.21 for a half-wave rectifier, producing significantly smoother DC. Option A (two diodes) describes a center-tapped full-wave rectifier — this is the most common confusion candidates make. Option D reverses that confusion: it is the center-tapped design (not the bridge) that requires a center-tapped transformer; the bridge works with any ordinary transformer. Option C (six diodes) applies to three-phase bridge rectifiers used in industrial power systems.

questions.stem: When a P-N junction diode is reverse-biased, a small current due to thermally generated minority carriers still flows through it. What is this current specifically called, and what is its defining characteristic?

options.option_text: Reverse saturation current; it stays nearly constant regardless of the reverse voltage
Reverse drift current; it increases proportionally as the reverse voltage is raised
Leakage diffusion current; majority carriers tunnel across the depletion region barrier
Zener current; strongly dependent on both temperature and the reverse bias magnitude

questions.explanation: A is correct. The reverse saturation current (I₀), also called dark current, is produced by thermally generated minority carriers swept across the junction by the built-in electric field. It is nearly independent of reverse voltage magnitude but approximately doubles for every 10°C temperature rise in silicon — a classic exam fact. Option B is wrong: drift is the transport mechanism, but the current does NOT scale with voltage; voltage-proportional increase only occurs near avalanche breakdown. Option C is wrong on two counts — it is minority carriers (not majority) and the transport mode is drift (not diffusion). Option D confuses this with Zener breakdown current, which is a distinct voltage-triggered phenomenon.

questions.stem: In a Bipolar Junction Transistor (BJT) operating in the active region, which expression correctly relates the emitter current (I_E), collector current (I_C), and base current (I_B)?

options.option_text: I_E equals I_C multiplied by I_B, linking all three BJT junction currents together
I_E equals the sum of I_C and I_B, as emitter supplies both collector and base paths
I_E equals I_C minus I_B, since base current partially opposes collector current flow
I_E approximately equals I_C alone, since I_B is negligibly small in all BJT designs

questions.explanation: B is correct. Applying Kirchhoff's Current Law at the BJT: the emitter injects carriers that either cross the base to reach the collector (I_C) or recombine within the base (I_B). Hence I_E = I_C + I_B. The dc current gain β = I_C/I_B, and α = I_C/I_E = β/(1+β). Option A (product) is a classic algebraic error with no physical basis. Option C (subtraction) is also wrong — all three currents are positive in the active region. Option D is approximately true for high-β transistors where I_B is small (β = 50–300), but it is not the exact relationship and fails in precision circuit analysis or when β is low.

questions.stem: A photodiode used as a light detector in a high-speed optical fibre communication system is typically operated under which biasing condition, and why is that condition preferred over the alternatives?

options.option_text: Forward bias; to lower junction barrier and allow photoexcited carriers to flow freely
Reverse bias; wider depletion region boosts light sensitivity and reduces response time
Zero bias (photovoltaic mode); operates on self-generated EMF without external supply
Forward bias; to increase minority carrier lifetime and amplify the photocurrent signal

questions.explanation: B is correct. Under reverse bias the depletion region widens, reducing junction capacitance and intensifying the electric field. This sweeps out photogenerated electron-hole pairs before recombination, producing fast, linear photocurrent proportional to light intensity — essential for Gb/s optical links. Option C (zero bias / photovoltaic mode) is valid for solar cells but has higher junction capacitance and slower response time, making it unsuitable for high-speed detection. Options A and D (forward bias) are incorrect: forward bias shrinks the depletion region, dramatically raises shot noise and dark current, and makes the device behave as an LED emitter, not a detector.

questions.stem: In an n-channel enhancement-mode MOSFET, when the gate-source voltage (V_GS) is kept below the threshold voltage (V_th), what is the state of the channel between source and drain terminals?

options.option_text: Fully conducting, allowing maximum current flow between drain and source terminals
Non-existent (no inversion layer), keeping the device in cut-off with near-zero current
Partially formed with reduced conductivity, giving a measurable subthreshold drain current
In depletion mode, the pre-formed channel carriers are repelled away by the gate field

questions.explanation: B is correct. An enhancement-mode MOSFET has no pre-formed channel at fabrication. Only when V_GS ≥ V_th does the gate field attract enough electrons to form an inversion layer connecting source to drain. Below V_th, no inversion layer exists and the device is in cut-off. Option C tempts candidates familiar with subthreshold conduction — real devices do exhibit exponentially decaying leakage below V_th — but standard circuit analysis treats the device as fully OFF below V_th; subthreshold is relevant only in ultra-low-power design. Option D confuses enhancement-mode with depletion-mode MOSFET: depletion-mode devices have a pre-formed channel that the gate voltage reduces, the opposite of enhancement-mode operation.

questions.stem: In a Hall effect experiment, an N-type semiconductor strip carries conventional current in the +x direction with a magnetic field applied in the +z direction. Which face of the strip accumulates negative charge, and what causes it?

options.option_text: The +y face becomes negative, as electrons are deflected upward by the magnetic force
The −y face becomes positive, as holes from the N-type material accumulate along it
The −y face becomes negative, as Lorentz-deflected electrons accumulate on that face
No net charge accumulates since N-type electrons and thermally generated holes cancel out

questions.explanation: C is correct. In N-type material, majority carriers are electrons. Conventional current in +x means electron drift velocity is in −x. The Lorentz force on electrons F = qv × B = (−e)(−v x̂) × (B ẑ) evaluates to force in the −y direction — electrons deflect toward the −y face. Electron accumulation makes the −y face negatively charged and the +y face positively charged. This polarity is the Hall effect signature identifying N-type material. For P-type, holes deflect to the −y face making it positive — the polarity reverses. Option A predicts negative charge at +y, which is the P-type polarity. Option B is doubly wrong: holes are minority carriers in N-type and would deflect to −y (positive, not negative) only in P-type. Option D ignores that N-type electrons overwhelmingly dominate over thermally generated minority holes.
